extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters; journalism students; trainee reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical handbook guidance for newspaper reporters on gathering local news, working beats, cultivating sources, and conducting interviews effectively and ethically. Covers routines, tools, preparation, and interpersonal techniques for on-the-street reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police slips and arrest sheets as primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short police 'slips' and 'arrest sheets' to get a brief but prompt and accurate account of accidents and crimes; the name signed is the reporting officer and the time indicates when the report was received at headquarters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest sheets are open to public inspection; abbreviations (M/S, R/W, D and D) indicate marital/education/charges; cases entered late may be unresolved. From these advance notices the reporter can follow up the event and obtain all available facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use institutional and official reporters (other news gatherers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctors, coroners, county clerks, recorders of deeds, building inspectors, hotel registers, etc., serve as non-paid news gatherers who must report births, deaths, licenses, transfers, condemned buildings, important guests, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly visit or monitor these offices because they maintain records (health department, coroner, county clerk, register of deeds, hospitals, police headquarters, etc.) that yield routine but newsworthy items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain beats (regular news runs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign and regularly cover specific 'beats' (runs) — places that serve as news sources — and know the kinds of news found at each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of beats and what to expect: Associated Charities (destitution, relief), Boards of Trade (market quotations), Coroner's Office (fatal accidents, murders), Fire Department (fires, losses), Health Department (births, contagious diseases), Shipping Offices (vessel departures, passenger lists), Labor Union HQ (labor news), etc. A reporter is held responsible for all news occurring on his run; neglect invites being scooped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate runs and respect responsibility for scoops
rubrics_metrics.description: On small papers one reporter may cover many runs; on large papers runs are distributed. The reporter is responsible for his run and will be penalized for being scooped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Police headquarters commonly provide one man (the 'watcher') who watches slips and telephones items to the city editor. Frequency of visits varies by beat; consistent attention is required. A scoop, even by minutes, is unacceptable to the city editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate 'dark runs' and discreet sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep certain consistently productive runs 'dark' — sources that produce exclusive facts but should be handled discreetly (garages, delicatessens, florists, caterers, mechanics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage friendships with tradesmen who may reveal private events (repairs, parties, crashes) that others won't know. Be aware of the unwritten etiquette of trade privacy; use tact to obtain exclusive facts without betraying confidences unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of wide acquaintance and maintaining integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately cultivate friendships and acquaintances on and off duty to gather items; personal and professional integrity is the reporter's first principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather useful items from a wide social circle (merchants, cabmen, clergy, barkeepers, patrolmen, porters). Do not betray confidences: publish news obtained on duty but avoid using confidential information from friends without express permission; publication decisions are for the city editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared when sent for a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Always carry cards, plenty of paper, pencils, and a neat engraved business card to facilitate admission and note-taking when sent to an unknown location (e.g., 'somebody at Grove and Spring has been shot').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep sharp, soft-lead pencils and folded copy paper for notes. Display of notebook and pencil should be minimal; a business card is often the only means of admittance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the telephone judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: The telephone is useful for running down rumors, tips, unimportant interviews, and stories subjects want to appear in the paper but is generally not advisable for important stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telephone cannot be trusted for serious reporting because one cannot see gestures and a person can easily end the call; use telephone to verify rumors (e.g., call a nearby bakery) but go in person for the main interview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your city and use maps when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult city maps to learn precise locations when uncertain, but aspire to know the city so well that maps are unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in a hurry, examine maps en route to transportation. Beginners should rely on maps while gaining local knowledge through experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the scene methodically (start with the policeman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon arrival at a scene, first consult the policeman on the beat; if he knows nothing, canvass adjacent houses and neighborhood shops systematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If early inquiries fail, check groceries, bakeries, saloons, meat markets, barber shops — customers or workers may recall partial details that lead to the person or place involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report progress regularly to the city editor
rubrics_metrics.description: While on assignment, maintain regular communication with the city editor, reporting progress frequently (some editors require hourly contact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular reports allow the editor to reassign resources, provide fuller information, and incorporate fresh details into frequent editions (especially for afternoon papers with hourly editions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrace work and exhaust available clues
rubrics_metrics.description: If initial searches fail, retrace inquiries: consult patrolmen, re-canvass houses, check laundries and corner shops to discover newcomers or overlooked witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laundry proprietors and housewives exchange information that can reveal new residents; do not leave until every plausible local clue has been followed up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination — never give up on a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Persist in investigating every available measure the circumstances permit; there is always some way to unearth a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact hospitals, question children playing nearby, revisit neighborhood shops; editors expect results, not excuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaining access for an interview (use cards, tact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a business card or polite inquiry to gain access to interview subjects in hotels, clubs, or private houses; adjust approach to the setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In hotels send a card via bellboy; at clubs give card to the porter; at modest homes simply inquire for the person. If access is denied, express interest and ask for cause as a natural segue toward the interview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six requirements for successful interviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly: (1) a pleasing presence, (2) ability to question judiciously, (3) quick perception of news in chance remarks, (4) retentive memory, (5) power to detect falsehood readily, and (6) ability to single out characteristic phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technically an interview is consultation for publishing opinions; in practice it means questioning any person to report his views. These attributes underpin the detailed interviewing techniques that follow (appearance, courtesy, questioning, memory, detection of falsehood, use of characteristic phrases).

rubrics_metrics.name: A pleasing presence (appearance and tact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immaculate personal appearance, clean linen, tact, and courtesy — qualities that put the interviewee at ease — are essential; lack of cleanliness or tact undermines success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unshaven faces or shabby collars; flattery is detected and resented. Clothing doesn't make a man but lack of it can ruin access; presence affects reception and the value of asked questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy in interviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Always act as a gentleman; never lose temper — anger causes loss of judgment and creates lasting hostility toward the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kindness begets kindness; maintain composure and tact to extract information and preserve future access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious questioning and letting subjects talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with topics that put the person at ease (often about their work), listen more than interrupt, guide conversation back when it strays, and avoid needless interruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the interviewee to speak at length; use silence strategically. If the subject veers off, gently steer back; be mindful of the 'personal equation' and adapt questioning style to the person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle persons seeking advertisement cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and avoid interviewees who want publicity for its own sake (those who 'talk' merely to see their names in print).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons will provide material but often supply self-promotional statements; avoid turning news columns into paid advertisement — advertising is sold, not editorially granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for dealing with refusals and eliciting secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: With those who refuse to talk, avoid provoking anger; with those who unwittingly divulge secrets, lead gradually away from the topic and circle back when they're off guard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be daunted by threats of legal action — gather facts and present them to the city editor. Subtly eliciting indiscreet statements is an advanced interviewing skill; observe without showing you noticed and record characteristic slips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick perception of news in chance remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop an immediate ability to recognize news value in offhand comments; missing such cues reveals ignorance and may prevent accurate recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control facial expressions and actions so you don't reveal that you've noticed something important; be ready to capture and record the remark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retentive memory for unnoted interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Many interviewees are intimidated by note-taking; reporters must retain facts mentally until they can record them accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some listen without notes and write later; others carry small cards or use cuff notes to capture phrases. Balance unobtrusive listening with accurate recording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use shorthand sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorthand is valuable for accuracy and recording exact statements but should not be overused as it can deaden presentation and produce lifeless copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorthand may cause the reporter to miss the spirit of the interview; use it 'as a walking cane, but not as a crutch.' Use for occasional exact quotations but not at the expense of capturing tone and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise, typewritten questions when exactness is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring a sheet of typewritten questions when exactness of statement is required — the subject must answer definitely or evade, either providing material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always have a clear purpose and precise questions in mind; busy or prominent people expect concise, purposeful visits and are irritated by vague interviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn the subject's career and background before interviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare by knowing a subject's career and accomplishments so the interviewee won't be asked to explain well-known incidents or technical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult files, encyclopedias, Who's Who, city editor, and local contacts. Preparation avoids wasting the subject's time and improves the quality and depth of answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to detect falsehood and assess motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that many interviewees speak with motives; few witnesses give unbiased accounts — the reporter must gauge mental caliber and possible motives for distortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider relationships, grudges, excitement levels, and reliability of witnesses. Failure to detect falsehood can lead to libel suits; corroborate important facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question everyone and seek multiple witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview everyone connected with a story — principals, witnesses, servants, janitors, chauffeurs, children — because each viewpoint may contribute vital facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humble witnesses often provide facts the responsible parties conceal; children are often less upset and more truthful. Corroborate accounts across sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check a person's previous record for identifying details
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquire into previous history (divorce, criminal record, prior incidents) as these items help identify characters and add useful context to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past events (previous fires, secret marriages, prior public notices) often illuminate current incidents and should be reported where relevant and verifiable.
